title: A MAN MARRIED HIS OWN SISTER—AND GOD STILL CHOSE THEIR SON TO LEAD ISRAEL?
paragraphs: A MAN MARRIED HIS OWN SISTER—AND GOD STILL CHOSE THEIR SON TO LEAD ISRAEL?

The shocking family secret behind Moses’ birth, the uncomfortable truth hidden in Exodus 6:20, and the breathtaking grace of a God who can bring deliverance out of a family history nobody would dare put on display.
What if I told you that one of the greatest deliverers in biblical history was born into a family relationship that God would later explicitly forbid?
Not a rumor.
Not an ancient conspiracy theory.
Not something invented to embarrass Christianity.
It is written in your Bible.
And the most unsettling part?
God did not erase the family record. He preserved it in Scripture.

Before Moses stood before Pharaoh, before the Red Sea opened, before the mountain shook with the presence of God, there was a marriage in his family that would make many modern readers deeply uncomfortable.
His father, Amram, married Jochebed.
And Jochebed was his father's sister.
His aunt.
Yes. You read that correctly.

But before you close your Bible in confusion, before someone uses this passage to mock Christianity, and before you conclude that God somehow approved of everything that happened in Moses' family, there is something extraordinarily important you need to understand.
Because this story is not about God celebrating a forbidden relationship.
It is about the difference between what Scripture records, what God commands, and what His grace can accomplish through deeply imperfect human histories.
And if you have ever looked at your own family, remembered something painful, and wondered whether your past disqualifies you from being used by God...
Stay with me.
There is something here for you.
Something that begins with a disturbing genealogy but leads us all the way to the cross of Jesus Christ.
Exodus 6:20 says:
“And Amram took him Jochebed his father's sister to wife; and she bare him Aaron and Moses: and the years of the life of Amram were an hundred and thirty and seven years.”
— Exodus 6:20, KJV
Read those words again.
“His father's sister.”
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
דֹּדָתוֹ — dodato
This means “his aunt,” specifically referring here to his father's sister.
The relevant Hebrew wording is:
וַיִּקַּח עַמְרָם אֶת־יוֹכֶבֶד דֹּדָתוֹ לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה
Vayyiqqach Amram et-Yokheved dodato lo le'ishah.
“And Amram took Jochebed, his aunt, as his wife.”
The Hebrew does not say that Amram married his biological sister.
It says he married his paternal aunt.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because sensationalism may attract attention, but biblical truth must govern what we teach.
Numbers 26:59 gives us another piece of the family history:
“And the name of Amram's wife was Jochebed, the daughter of Levi, whom her mother bare to Levi in Egypt: and she bare unto Amram Aaron and Moses, and Miriam their sister.”
— Numbers 26:59, KJV
Jochebed belonged to Levi's family. Amram was descended from Levi through Kohath.
Under the straightforward reading of these genealogies, Jochebed was Amram's paternal aunt.
And from this marriage came three names that would become inseparable from Israel's deliverance.
Miriam.
Aaron.
Moses.
A prophetess associated with Israel's song of victory.
A priest who would become Israel's first high priest.
And a man whom God would call to confront the most powerful ruler in Egypt.
But now comes the question that makes this account so difficult.
Didn't God later forbid this exact kind of marriage?
Yes.
And the Bible does not hide that either.
Leviticus 18:12 declares:
“Thou shalt not uncover the nakedness of thy father's sister: she is thy father's near kinswoman.”
— Leviticus 18:12, KJV
Leviticus 20:19 also prohibits sexual relations involving a father's sister or mother's sister.
These are not vague restrictions.
They address the precise degree of family relationship described in Exodus 6:20.
So how do we understand this?
How could Moses come from a marriage involving his father's sister when the Law later delivered through Moses would forbid such a union?
Here is where careful reading becomes essential.
Amram and Jochebed's marriage took place before the Mosaic Law was given at Sinai.
The explicit prohibitions in Leviticus were delivered to Israel later, after the exodus from Egypt.
This chronological difference helps explain why the narrative records the marriage without pausing to apply the later legal penalty to Amram and Jochebed.
But we must be careful.
The fact that a marriage occurred before the giving of a particular command does not automatically prove that God morally approved of it.
Nor does the Bible tell us that God praised their marriage.
Scripture simply records the relationship.
It does not provide a detailed moral evaluation of their union.
And that distinction is crucial.
The Bible's honesty about what happened is not the same as God's endorsement of everything that happened.
Think about that.
Scripture records Abraham's deception.
Jacob's manipulation.
David's adultery.
Solomon's disobedience.
Peter's denial.
And Judas's betrayal.
Yet the presence of those events in Scripture never means God approved of them.
Sometimes the Bible tells us what people did so that we can understand the history of redemption, not so that we can imitate every decision they made.
And there is another important truth.
The Bible does not present Moses as the leader of Israel because his parents' marriage was exceptional.
God called Moses according to His redemptive purpose.
The story is not an invitation to justify incestuous relationships today.
The biblical prohibitions against close-kin sexual unions remain serious moral boundaries.
Grace is never permission to redefine what God calls sin.
But grace does mean that human brokenness cannot automatically defeat God's purposes.
Now imagine the world into which Moses was born.
Egypt.
A nation of towering monuments, magnificent palaces, and merciless oppression.
The Israelites were suffering under forced labor.
Their cries were rising toward heaven.
And Pharaoh had issued a terrifying command.
Hebrew baby boys were to be killed.
Imagine being a mother in that world.
You have just given birth.
You hold your child against your chest.
You study his tiny fingers.
You listen to his breathing.
And somewhere outside your home, soldiers have the authority to take his life.
Every cry could expose him.
Every passing footstep could mean danger.
Every knock at the door could become a nightmare.
That was Jochebed's world.
Exodus 2:2 tells us that she hid her baby for three months.
Three months of fear.
Three months of whispered prayers.
Three months of trying to keep a newborn quiet while an empire hunted children like him.
Can you imagine that?
A mother pressing her baby close, perhaps trembling every time he cried.
A father wondering how much longer they could protect him.
A sister watching everything unfold, too young to change the world but old enough to understand that her little brother's life was in danger.
And then the day came when hiding him was no longer possible.
Jochebed prepared a basket.
She waterproofed it.
She placed her son inside.
And she set it among the reeds by the Nile.
Try to picture her hands.
The same hands that had held him.
Fed him.
Comforted him.
Now carefully releasing the basket that carried everything she desperately wanted to protect.
The Bible does not record her private thoughts or exact prayers.
But it tells us what she did.
And Hebrews 11:23 later remembers the faith and courage of Moses' parents.
They were not simply surrendering their child to chance.
They were resisting a murderous royal command.
And into that terrifying moment, God's providence was already at work.
Pharaoh's daughter came to the river.
She discovered the child.
She recognized him as a Hebrew baby.
And she had compassion.
Then Miriam, watching nearby, approached with a remarkable question.
Could she find a Hebrew woman to nurse the child?
The princess agreed.
And the woman who was summoned was Jochebed herself.
The mother who had released her child into the river was given the opportunity to nurse and care for him.
Read Exodus 2:1–10.
The beauty of that moment is almost overwhelming.
The king had ordered Hebrew sons to die.
Yet a Hebrew son was rescued through the compassion of the king's own daughter.
The mother who could no longer hide him was allowed to care for him.
And the child who should have been killed would one day stand before Pharaoh with God's command:
“Let my people go.”
Do you see it?
The empire believed it controlled the future.
But God was preparing a deliverer right under Pharaoh's roof.
And here is what makes this story deeply personal.
Moses did not enter history with a family background that modern readers would consider uncomplicated.
His ancestry contained a relationship that would later be prohibited under Israel's Law.
His people were enslaved.
His infancy was threatened.
His childhood involved separation and adoption into an Egyptian royal household.
And later, Moses himself would commit a serious act of violence.
Exodus 2:12 records that he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew man.
Moses then fled.
The man who would eventually confront Pharaoh first became a fugitive.
The future leader spent years away from the place where his calling would unfold.
And when God finally called him from the burning bush, Moses did not respond like a fearless hero.
He questioned his own ability.
“Who am I, that I should go unto Pharaoh?”
— Exodus 3:11, KJV
Who am I?
Four words.
But perhaps you know what they feel like.
Who am I to serve God after what I have done?
Who am I to speak about Jesus when my own family has so many problems?
Who am I to encourage others when I still struggle?
Who am I to pray when I have failed so many times?
Who am I to believe God could use me when I can barely forgive myself?
Some people carry shame that began long before they made their own decisions.
They grew up in families marked by addiction.
Infidelity.
Abandonment.
Violence.
Secrets.
Broken promises.
Generational conflict.
Some were told they were unwanted.
Some were blamed for circumstances they never created.
Some learned to hide their family history because they feared that if people knew the truth, they would never be accepted.
And perhaps that is why the genealogy of Moses matters more than we first realize.
Because God did not need to rewrite Moses' ancestry into a spotless family history before calling him.
But listen carefully.
That does not mean family trauma is good.
It does not mean harmful relationships should be defended.
It does not mean we should romanticize sin, excuse abuse, or ignore the consequences of destructive choices.
It means that a person's family history is not the final authority over that person's future.
Your parents' failures are not automatically your guilt.
Your family's reputation is not your identity.
And the circumstances surrounding your birth do not determine your worth before God.
Ezekiel 18:20 teaches personal moral responsibility, declaring that the son does not bear the guilt of the father merely because he is his son.
That truth matters.
Especially to someone who has spent years carrying shame that was never theirs to carry.
But there is something even greater than the story of Moses.
Because Moses was never meant to be the final answer.
He was a deliverer.
But he was not the ultimate Deliverer.
He confronted Pharaoh.
But he could not conquer the power of sin and death.
He led Israel out of Egypt.
But he could not, by his own righteousness, bring humanity into eternal reconciliation with God.
He mediated the old covenant.
But another would come who would be greater.
Jesus Christ.
And here is where this entire story turns from uncomfortable genealogy into breathtaking Gospel hope.
God did not save Israel because Moses came from a flawless family. And God does not save us because we come from flawless families either.
Our salvation rests on Jesus Christ.
Not our pedigree.
Not our reputation.
Not our achievements.
Not the absence of scandal in our family tree.
But the finished work of the crucified and risen Savior.
Consider the opening of Matthew's Gospel.
Before Matthew tells us about the birth of Jesus, he presents a genealogy.
And that genealogy contains stories that are anything but sanitized.
Judah and Tamar.
Rahab.
Ruth.
David and the wife of Uriah.
Their circumstances were not identical, and their stories must not be carelessly reduced to the same moral category.
But together they remind us that the biblical history leading to the Messiah was not a parade of morally flawless people.
Matthew 1:6 even identifies Solomon's mother by reference to Uriah, recalling one of David's darkest chapters.
Why preserve such painful history?
The text does not explain every reason.
But it certainly does not hide the past.
And when we reach the end of that genealogy, we encounter the One who changes everything.
Jesus.
The Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The Savior who entered a world already scarred by human sin.
He did not come because humanity had finally cleaned itself up.
He came because sinners needed saving.
Matthew 1:21 declares:
“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from public criticism.
Not merely from the consequences of a ruined reputation.
From their sins.
That is the Gospel.
And it is far more powerful than a motivational message about overcoming a difficult past.
Because the Gospel does not simply tell us that we are stronger than our history.
It tells us that Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
The New Testament expresses this beautifully in Ephesians 2:8–9:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
The Greek word translated “grace” is:
χάρις — charis
Grace.
God's undeserved favor.
Not a reward for an impressive family history.
Not a prize for having avoided every mistake.
Not something purchased by religious performance.
A gift.
And the Greek word translated “saved” in Ephesians 2:8 is:
σεσῳσμένοι — sesōsmenoi
A perfect passive participle from the verb sōzō, meaning “to save.”
In this construction, it describes believers as having been saved, with the resulting condition continuing.
The emphasis is not on sinners rescuing themselves.
It is on God's saving action received through faith.
And that changes the way we look at our lives.
Because some of us are still trying to earn what Christ offers by grace.
We think if we pray enough, serve enough, give enough, suffer enough, or prove ourselves enough, God might finally accept us.
But the cross announces something altogether different.
Jesus did not die so that we could purchase forgiveness through good behavior.
He died because we could never make ourselves righteous before God through our own efforts.
And He rose again, demonstrating His victory over sin and death.
This is why the Gospel cannot be reduced to the slogan that God uses imperfect people.
That statement is true, but it is incomplete.
The deeper truth is that God saves guilty sinners through the perfect righteousness, sacrificial death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
And the grace that saves us also calls us to change.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not tell us to remain comfortable in sin.
Grace calls us out of darkness.
Grace confronts what destroys us.
Grace leads us toward repentance.
Grace teaches us to forgive.
Grace empowers a new way of living.
And this brings us back to Amram and Jochebed.
Their family relationship is not a model for Christian marriage.
Their genealogy is not permission to ignore biblical sexual boundaries.
And the later prohibitions in Leviticus must not be dismissed simply because Moses came from that family.
But neither should we pretend that the Bible's difficult family histories somehow make God's redemptive work impossible.
God's holiness remains holy.
His commands remain serious.
His mercy remains astonishing.
And His sovereign purposes are not defeated by the imperfections of human ancestry.
Now I want to ask you something.
Not as someone looking for a dramatic reaction.
But as someone who knows that behind every screen is a real person carrying a story.
What part of your history have you allowed to convince you that God could never use your life?
Was it something your parents did?
A broken marriage?
A childhood you rarely talk about?
A decision you regret?
A season when you walked away from God?
A secret that still makes you feel ashamed?
Maybe you have been attending church while quietly believing you are less worthy than everyone sitting beside you.
You sing about forgiveness.
But struggle to believe it applies to you.
You tell others that Jesus changes lives.
But wonder whether yours is too damaged.
You encourage people to trust God's promises.
Then return home and stare at the ceiling, wondering why your own heart still feels so heavy.
Listen.
You do not have to pretend your past was harmless.
You do not have to call evil good.
You do not have to minimize what someone did to you.
And you do not have to manufacture a beautiful testimony before coming to Jesus.
Come truthfully.
Come repentantly where you have sinned.
Come wounded where you have been hurt.
Come weary where life has exhausted you.
Come trusting the Savior who said:
“Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.”
— Matthew 11:28, KJV
He did not say, “Come when your family tree is perfect.”
He did not say, “Come when nobody remembers your mistakes.”
He did not say, “Come after you have repaired every broken piece of your life.”
He said, “Come unto me.”
And perhaps those are the words you have needed to hear for a very long time.
Not because God overlooks sin.
But because Jesus is the Savior sinners desperately need.
Not because a comment saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But because sometimes an honest expression of need opens the door for another believer to encourage you, pray with you, and remind you of the promises of God.
Your story may help someone who feels completely alone.
There may be someone reading quietly who has not prayed in months.
Someone who still believes in God but has stopped believing that mercy is possible for them.
Someone who thinks the failures of their parents have permanently ruined their future.
Someone who needs to know that the Bible does not hide complicated families—and that the Gospel offers something greater than a perfect reputation.
Not merely because it is surprising.
Not because scandal generates attention.
But because biblical truth deserves to travel farther than misinformation, shame, and despair.
Sometimes the most loving thing we can do is make sure someone encounters the truth of Jesus Christ at the moment they need it.
There may come a day when your own past starts speaking louder than God's promises.
Return to the Scriptures.
Remember the difference between God's commands and the human failures recorded in biblical history.
Remember that your identity is not established by your family's worst chapter.
And above all, remember that Jesus Christ is the only sufficient foundation for forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn the Bible into sensational entertainment.
Not to build a following around controversy.
Not to promise that every painful story will end exactly as we wish.
But to help people open Scripture, encounter the truth, repent of sin, grow in faith, and follow Jesus Christ with greater understanding and devotion.
And if this message has strengthened you, I want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical teaching and spiritual nourishment more accessible to people who are hungry for God's Word.
You can help that work continue.
Think of it as a voluntary monthly ministry offering—a practical expression of generosity toward work you believe is helping others encounter the Gospel.
But I want to make something very clear.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
It does not replace your responsibility to care for your family or the faithful support of your local church.
And it should not be confused with a biblically mandated tithe.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Cheerfully.
Without pressure or guilt.
Jesus is.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Invite others.
Make use of the free resources.
Because the message of salvation must never be treated as something that can be purchased.
There is so much confusion about Scripture.
So much shallow teaching.
So much pain hidden behind smiling faces.
People need more than another religious slogan.
They need the Word of God understood faithfully.
They need the truth about sin and repentance.
They need the hope of forgiveness.
They need to know Jesus Christ.
And now, before we finish, return with me one last time to that little Hebrew baby by the Nile.
A basket.
A river.
A death sentence.
A watching sister.
A grieving, courageous mother.
An Egyptian princess.
And a future that no one standing beside that river could fully see.
The baby would grow.
The fugitive would be called.
The reluctant man would confront Pharaoh.
The sea would part.
The people would walk toward freedom.
And generations later, another Deliverer would come.
Not to rescue Israel from Pharaoh, but to accomplish a redemption far greater than the exodus from Egypt.
Jesus Christ would bear the sins of His people.
He would suffer on the cross.
He would rise from the dead.
And through Him, all who repent and believe receive the forgiveness and life that no human leader could ever provide.
Moses' story was remarkable.
But Moses was not the center of God's final answer to human sin.
Jesus is.
And that is the most important thing to remember when reading any difficult passage in Scripture.
The Bible is not ultimately a collection of stories about perfect people.
It is the unfolding revelation of the holy God who keeps His promises and brings redemption to sinners through His Son.
So when you read Exodus 6:20 again, do not deny the uncomfortable details.
Do not exaggerate them.
Do not turn them into permission for what Scripture forbids.
And do not miss the greater story of God's faithfulness.
The same Bible that honestly records the complicated ancestry of Moses also reveals the spotless Savior who came to redeem sinners.
That is why we can speak about scandal without glorifying it.
That is why we can speak about grace without cheapening it.
That is why we can confront sin without declaring any repentant sinner beyond the reach of Christ.
And that is why your story does not have to end where your shame began.
Because perhaps the most important thing about your life is not what happened before you knew Jesus.
Perhaps it is what Jesus is doing now as you learn to follow Him.
Your family history may explain where your story began, but only Jesus Christ can redeem you—and your past does not get to overrule His promise of grace.
